reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / standard metabolic references
clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficiency of the enzyme lysosomal acid lipase, leading to accumulation of cholesteryl esters and triglycerides within lysosomes
Wolman disease is the severe infantile end of the spectrum, presenting in the first weeks of life with vomiting, diarrhoea, and failure to thrive
Marked hepatosplenomegaly with progressive liver dysfunction is a prominent feature
Bilateral adrenal enlargement with calcification is a characteristic and helpful imaging clue
Malabsorption and steatorrhoea contribute to profound failure to thrive and early death if untreated
The milder, later-onset variant caused by the same enzyme deficiency is cholesteryl ester storage disease, presenting with hepatomegaly and dyslipidaemia
A dyslipidaemic profile with elevated LDL cholesterol and low HDL is typical, reflecting impaired lipid handling
Enzyme replacement therapy is available for lysosomal acid lipase deficiency, and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation has been used in selected cases, alongside nutritional support
reference.pathophysiology: Wolman disease is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in LIPA, encoding lysosomal acid lipase, the enzyme that hydrolyses cholesteryl esters and triglycerides delivered to the lysosome. Deficient activity causes these lipids to accumulate within lysosomes of the liver, spleen, intestine, adrenal glands, and macrophages throughout the body. Massive lipid storage produces hepatosplenomegaly, hepatic dysfunction, adrenal infiltration with calcification, and intestinal involvement causing malabsorption. Disrupted intracellular cholesterol sensing also drives a proatherogenic dyslipidaemia. The severe infantile phenotype reflects near-absent enzyme activity, whereas residual activity underlies the milder cholesteryl ester storage disease.
additionalDifferentials: Other lysosomal storage disorders with hepatosplenomegaly such as Niemann-Pick disease
Other causes of neonatal failure to thrive with malabsorption
Infantile cholestatic and metabolic liver disease
Familial hyperlipidaemias for the milder phenotype
Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease in later-onset presentations
additionalInvestigations: Assay of lysosomal acid lipase enzyme activity, including dried blood spot testing
LIPA molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis
Abdominal imaging demonstrating hepatosplenomegaly and adrenal calcification
Liver function tests and fasting lipid profile
Assessment of nutrition, growth, and malabsorption
redFlags: Profound failure to thrive with vomiting and diarrhoea in early infancy
Progressive liver dysfunction or hepatic failure
Adrenal insufficiency associated with adrenal involvement
Severe malabsorption with rapid clinical deterioration
reference.prognosis: Untreated infantile Wolman disease is rapidly progressive and usually fatal within the first months of life. Enzyme replacement therapy has substantially improved survival in this severe form, and the later-onset cholesteryl ester storage disease has a more chronic course dominated by liver disease and dyslipidaemia with associated cardiovascular risk.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnosis in a neonate with failure to thrive and hepatosplenomegaly
Missing adrenal calcification on imaging as a diagnostic pointer
Failing to recognise the milder cholesteryl ester storage disease as the same enzyme deficiency
Delaying enzyme replacement therapy, which is most beneficial when started early
management: Enzyme replacement therapy with recombinant lysosomal acid lipase (sebelipase alfa) is the disease-specific treatment and has transformed survival in the severe infantile form
Nutritional support with a modified low-fat regimen and parenteral nutrition to counter malabsorption, steatorrhoea and profound failure to thrive
Lipid-lowering therapy such as a statin with ezetimibe for the proatherogenic dyslipidaemia, particularly in the milder cholesteryl ester storage disease spectrum
Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation considered in selected cases as an alternative disease-directed approach
Monitoring of liver function, growth, nutritional status and adrenal function given adrenal infiltration and calcification
Multidisciplinary metabolic care with escalation for hepatic failure
Genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive LIPA disorder, with family screening
